title: Sent Out, and Who Is My Neighbor
overview: Jesus sends out a larger group of followers ahead of him, then teaches through a prayer, a story about a Samaritan, and a visit to two sisters what really matters.

parts.label: Seventy-two sent ahead (vv. 1-12)
parts.note: Old manuscripts say either seventy or seventy-two, a number that may echo Moses' seventy elders or the nations listed in Genesis 10, and these followers were told to travel light, accept whatever hospitality they were given, and skip long roadside greetings because the task was urgent. Wiping a town's dust off their feet was a public sign of breaking ties with a place that refused them.

parts.label: Warning to Galilean towns (vv. 13-16)
parts.note: Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum were towns where Jesus had done much of his work, while Tyre, Sidon and Sodom were outsider cities remembered for wealth or wickedness. His point is that those who saw the most and still shrugged it off carry the heavier responsibility.

parts.label: Return and Jesus' joy (vv. 17-24)
parts.note: Jesus' words about seeing Satan fall like lightning seem to mean their small successes were a sign that evil's grip was breaking, though the exact sense is debated, and he says the deeper reason for joy is belonging to God, not having power. He then thanks God that ordinary people grasped what the learned missed, and Christians read verse 22 as Jesus claiming a unique knowledge of God that only he can share.

parts.label: A lawyer's test (vv. 25-29)
parts.note: An expert in the religious law sums it up with two lines from Israel's scriptures: love God fully and love your neighbor as yourself. Wanting to look good, he then asks where the line falls on who counts as a neighbor.

parts.label: The good Samaritan (vv. 30-37)
parts.note: On a dangerous desert road, two temple officials pass a beaten man without stopping, and the text gives no reason, though some suggest fear of becoming ritually unclean. The one who helps, spending about two days' wages on him, is a Samaritan, from a neighboring people long locked in hostility with Jews, and Jesus turns the question from 'who qualifies as my neighbor' to 'who acts like one.'

parts.label: Martha and Mary (vv. 38-42)
parts.note: Mary sits at Jesus' feet, the posture of a student, which many scholars see as unusual for a woman at the time, while Martha wears herself out hosting. Jesus does not scorn Martha's work but says that listening to him is the one thing that matters most.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the Samaritan story is mainly a moral example of how to treat others or also a picture of Jesus himself rescuing wounded humanity, as many early church writers read it.
think: Who is the person you would least expect help from, and how would it feel if they were the one who stopped for you?
